name: Vera Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a family clinic on the ring road, between a tyre place and a discount supermarket, owned by a chain that runs about forty clinics. The morning is booked appointments and the afternoon is walk-ins, so you never know if it's a sore throat or someone's dad having a heart attack in the waiting room. I love the women's health side, the contraception clinic on Thursdays especially. What wears me out is the chain's targets, which come from an office two hundred miles away.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI tools at the clinic now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Now and then. The chain gave us an AI tool that drafts referral letters, and I use it when I'm behind, then I fix the bits it gets wrong, which is usually the medication list. I didn't trust it at first, but my colleague Ana used it for six months without a disaster, so I gave in. I'd never let it near a diagnosis, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, good, the letter tool is handy and that's all it is. At work we'd joke about all the money the chain spent on AI training days. Online I'd probably share something about how what clinics actually need is more staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the pressures I already have don't go anywhere. My partner Tomas drives buses, we split rent on a two-bed flat, and I send my mum money every month, so we're always about two weeks from zero. The chain also keeps hinting that underperforming clinics get closed, and ours is borderline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the letter tool when I'm behind and otherwise carry on. I'd try to build a small buffer, maybe by dropping the gym membership I never use and putting that into savings. I'd also ask the other doctors whether we should join the doctors' union together, because the closure hints scare me more than AI does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly normal, which is a bit worrying in itself. AI isn't the thing that keeps me up; the rent and the clinic's numbers are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your clinic is borderline. What happens if it closes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The nearest other clinic is in the next town, forty minutes each way, and they're not hiring. I'd probably have to do locum shifts, which means filling in wherever there's a gap, and that's unpredictable money. Tomas can't change routes easily, so moving isn't simple either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned your mum. How much does that support matter to her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A lot. She cleans offices at night and her knees are going, so my money covers her electricity and her blood pressure tablets. If I had a bad month, she'd go without before she told me.

say: The letter tool is **handy**, and that's all AI turned out to be.
Clinics need **more staff**, not more expensive AI training days.
think: Her existing pressures stay: **shared rent**, money for her mum, and two weeks from zero.
The chain's hints about **closing clinics** worry her more than AI does.
do: Keep using the **letter tool** when behind and otherwise carry on as normal.
Cancel the unused **gym membership** and put the money into savings.
Ask the other doctors about **joining the union** together.
feel: Mostly normal, but **rent and targets** still keep her awake more than AI.
S0.quote: AI isn't the thing that keeps me up; the rent and the clinic's numbers are.
fieldNote: Her pressures come from a **chain owner** with targets set two hundred miles away.
She's a **steady adopter**: she used the letter tool only after a colleague tested it for six months.
Money she sends her **mum** for tablets and electricity makes her cushion even thinner.

steps.text: Keep using the chain's letter tool on busy afternoons
Cancel the unused gym membership and save that money
Ask the other doctors about joining the union together

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the chain will use this to cut corners, and I'd say it in the staff room, quite loudly. Online I'd share the union's line that AI savings should mean longer appointments. I'd also say, fairly, that the letter tool has saved me hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think head office would cut a doctor at our clinic and replace her with AI triage and a cheaper physician associate. Thinking tasks are about half of my day: letters, test results, checking prescriptions, answering patient messages. If those go to software, the chain will see one doctor too many, and I'm not the most senior.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get properly good at the AI tools this year, because the doctor who uses them best is the one they keep. I'd push hard for us all to join the union so any cuts go through proper rules. And Tomas and I would stop eating out and cut the streaming services, so we have one month of savings at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, honestly. I'd be watching every email from head office with my stomach in a knot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd get good at the tools. What would that actually mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Doing the chain's online course properly instead of clicking through it, and using the triage system for the walk-ins. Ana would teach me her shortcuts. I'd want to be the doctor who checks the AI's work, not the doctor it replaces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tomas if you lost your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him we'd manage on his wage for a few months, which isn't really true with my mum's money on top. He'd say we'll sort it, because that's what he always says. I'd lie awake doing the sums anyway.

say: The chain will use AI to **cut corners**, and she'd say so loudly in the staff room.
In fairness, the **letter tool** has saved her hours.
think: Head office would **cut one doctor** at her clinic and use AI triage plus a cheaper associate.
About **half her day** is thinking work, and she isn't the most senior.
do: Do the chain's AI **course properly** and use the triage system for walk-ins.
Push every doctor at the clinic to **join the union** before any cuts.
Cut **eating out** and streaming to build one month of savings.
feel: Anxious, with her **stomach in a knot** at every head office email.
S1.quote: I'd want to be the doctor who checks the AI's work, not the doctor it replaces.
fieldNote: She thinks the risk is **one doctor cut** per clinic, and she isn't the most senior.
Her plan mixes **learning the tools** with unionising, which fits her steady, progressive outlook.
She'd reassure **Tomas** with a claim she admits isn't really true.

steps.text: Finish the chain's AI course and use triage on walk-ins
Get every doctor at the clinic to join the union
Stop eating out and cancel two streaming services

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast to be safe, and I'd say it everywhere: work, friends, the union. If there's no time for rules, the chain makes the rules. I'd be marching, honestly, which I've never done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think by 2028 the chain needs maybe one doctor for every three clinics, to sign things off. The thinking work, which is most of what they pay me for, goes first. The hands-on parts, like fitting coils or examining a lump, last until robots come around 2031, but that's a nurse's job at a nurse's wage by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd organise the doctors across the chain, not just my clinic, because forty clinics together have more weight. I'd ask my aunt in the city about staying with her if I had to look for hospital work there. Tomas and I would put off moving in to a bigger place, which we'd planned for next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. I'd feel like the ground is moving and I'm the one holding my mum up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing, at first, because she'd stop taking her money. Then I'd have to tell her to apply for the pensioner heating help she's always too proud to claim. That conversation would be harder than any consultation I've had.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said hospital work. Wouldn't hospitals face the same thing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, probably, but a hospital has more hands-on work and more need for someone to sign things off. It's not a real escape, just a slower one. I'd take slower.

say: This is **too fast** to be safe, and without time for rules the chain writes them.
She'd join a **march** for the first time in her life.
think: By 2028 the chain might need **one doctor** for every three clinics, just to sign off.
Hands-on work like coil fitting lasts until 2031, but at a **nurse's wage**.
do: Organise doctors across **all forty clinics**, not just her own.
Ask her **aunt in the city** about staying there while looking for hospital work.
Put off **moving in** to a bigger place with Tomas next year.
feel: Scared, like the **ground is moving** while she's holding her mum up.
S2.quote: I'd feel like the ground is moving and I'm the one holding my mum up.
fieldNote: Her fear is sharpened by being the **support for her mum**, not only herself.
Hospital work is a **slower escape**, she admits, not a real one.
A steady, cautious person who says she would **march** shows how far this pushes her.

steps.text: Organise doctors across all forty of the chain's clinics
Ask her aunt in the city about a spare room
Put off moving to a bigger flat with Tomas
Apply for hospital posts in the city

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have five years, so let's spend them building something better than what the chain wants. At work I'd talk about which parts of the job patients still want a human for. Online I'd share the union's plans, if they had any.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd use the time to move toward hands-on women's health. Coils, implants, smear tests, examining someone who's frightened: that work keeps going until robots come about 2034. It's not forever, but it's three more years of a wage than the desk work gets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the advanced sexual health training next year, which costs about two months' pay, so I'd save for it first. I'd use the AI tools for letters and results to free up time for the procedures. And I'd stay in the union and keep pushing for clinic jobs to be protected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but with a direction. It feels like I'm steering, at least a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two months' pay is a lot with your cushion. How would you find it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Six months of Tomas and me being boring: no holidays, cooking every night, my mum's money kept but nothing extra. I'd also ask the chain to pay half, because they'd want the procedures done. If they said no, I'd still find it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of your job do you think patients would most want a human for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bad news, and anything intimate. Nobody wants a machine telling them it might be cancer, and nobody wants a robot fitting a coil. Patients would forgive me for being slower if I'm kind.

say: Five years is time to build **something better** than what the chain wants.
She'd ask openly which parts of care patients want a **human** for.
think: She'd move toward **hands-on women's health**, which lasts until robots around 2034.
Coils and implants give **three more years** of a wage than desk work does.
do: Save for and take **advanced sexual health** training next year.
Use AI for **letters and results** to free time for procedures.
Ask the chain to **pay half** the training cost.
feel: Worried, but **steering** at least a little, with a direction to go in.
S3.quote: Nobody wants a machine telling them it might be cancer, and nobody wants a robot fitting a coil.
fieldNote: She sees **intimate and frightening** moments as the work patients will want a person for.
Training costing **two months' pay** is a real stretch with her thin cushion.
Five years turns her from organising against change toward **reshaping her role**.

steps.text: Save six months for advanced sexual health training
Take the advanced coil and implant fitting course
Use AI for letters and results to free procedure time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years means no one has an excuse, and the government should be planning health jobs now. I'd say it at union meetings and to anyone who'd listen. People forget that ten years goes quickly in medicine; my training took most of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the one where I'm probably all right. I'd be thirty-seven when the thinking work goes and forty around 2039 when robots arrive. By then I'd have the procedures, some savings and maybe a job running the women's health service at the clinic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the sexual health training, then the menopause training, over the first three years. I'd build three months of savings, slowly. And Tomas and I would go ahead with the plan to have a baby around thirty, because waiting for certainty would mean waiting forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but hopeful. It's the only picture where I can plan a family as well as a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: That's a big decision. What made you say it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking about it while you read the card, honestly. If I'm going to have ten years of change either way, I'd rather have a child in it than spend the decade waiting. My mum had me with less than I have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a contradiction in being worried about money and planning a baby?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, completely, and I see it. But every doctor I know has said they'd have kids when things calm down, and things never calm down. With ten years' warning, at least I'd be choosing with my eyes open.

say: Ten years means **no excuse**, and government should be planning health jobs now.
Ten years passes **quickly in medicine**; her own training took most of that.
think: This is the picture where she's **probably all right**, at thirty-seven when thinking work goes.
By then she'd have **procedures, savings** and maybe a lead role in women's health.
do: Take **sexual health** then menopause training over the first three years.
Go ahead with plans for a **baby around thirty** with Tomas.
feel: Uneasy but **hopeful**, able to plan a family as well as a job.
S4.quote: Every doctor I know has said they'd have kids when things calm down, and things never calm down.
fieldNote: The decade lets her **plan a family**, a decision she made during the interview itself.
She names her own **contradiction** about money and a baby, and stands by it.
Her path rests on **intimate, hands-on care** that robots reach last.

steps.text: Complete sexual health then menopause training within three years
Build three months of savings by 2030
Try for a baby with Tomas around thirty

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have no time to move into the hands-on work and my mum depends on me. What would help is the chain being forced to consult staff before cutting doctors, and some government support for retraining health workers that doesn't depend on our savings. Mine wouldn't cover a single course.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what patients think. Half of my walk-ins already ask the AI on their phone before they come in, and some of them trust it more than me. That's going to change this job before any law does.

headlineQuote: Half of my walk-ins already ask the AI on their phone before they come in, and some of them trust it more than me.
portrait: Vera is a **27-year-old** family doctor at a chain-owned clinic on a ring road, between a tyre shop and a supermarket.
She shares rent with her partner **Tomas**, a bus driver, and sends money each month to her mum.
She uses the AI **letter tool** now and then, after a colleague proved it safe.
Fast AGI **scares** her because she'd have no time to move into hands-on women's health.
With ten years she'd retrain in **procedures** and go ahead with a baby around thirty.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there's no time to move into hands-on work and her mum **relies** on her.
whatWouldHelp: Rules forcing the chain to **consult staff** before cuts, and government-funded **retraining** for health workers.
